The data cover 197 countries and 12 country groups from 1980 to 2031, from the
IMF's *World Economic Outlook* (October 2026), including the IMF's projections for the coming years. Hover
over a chart to read its values, compare up to five countries or groups, draw a benchmark as a gray
reference line, hide or show the projections, and open the Python code under any chart to rebuild it in
Google Colab.

These snapshots look at the **short run and economic policy**: business cycles, inflation, unemployment,
government budgets and debt, and the external accounts. Their companion, the
[PWT Snapshots](pwt-snapshots.html), follows the **long run** of every country with the Penn World Table.

[← Back to the book](../index.html)

## Explore {#explore}

Each question opens the page on the countries, years and chart it is about.

::: {.snap-explore}
1. **The Covid-19 recession.** In 2020, real GDP fell in the world as a whole. Which fell more, the advanced economies or the emerging and developing economies, and which bounced back faster? [Try it →](#c=G110,G200,G001&y=2015-2031&p=growth){.snap-try}
2. **The inflation surge.** Inflation jumped in 2021-2022 in the United States, the United Kingdom and the euro area. How high did it go, and what did Japan, after decades of near-zero inflation, see? [Try it →](#c=USA,GBR,G163,JPN&y=2015-2031&p=infl){.snap-try}
3. **High inflation.** Argentina's inflation passed 200% in 2024. What does the IMF project for the next years? [Try it →](#c=ARG&y=2010-2031&p=infl){.snap-try}
4. **Two labor markets in the Great Recession.** Compare unemployment in Spain and Germany after 2008: why did one rise to more than 25% while the other kept falling? [Try it →](#c=ESP,DEU&y=2000-2031&p=unemp){.snap-try}
5. **Greece's crisis.** Follow Greece's real GDP growth and government debt from 2005: how many years did output fall, and how high did the debt ratio climb? [Try it →](#c=GRC&y=2005-2031&p=debt){.snap-try}
6. **Output gaps.** In which years was US output above its potential (a positive gap), and how deep was the gap in 2009 and 2020? [Try it →](#c=USA&y=2000-2031&p=gap){.snap-try}
7. **Japan's debt.** Japan's gross government debt is above 200% of GDP. Compare it with Italy, the United States and the advanced economies, then switch to net debt above the chart. [Try it →](#c=JPN,ITA,USA,G110&p=debt){.snap-try}
8. **Saving more than investing.** China saves more than 40% of its GDP. Is its saving above its investment, and what does that imply for its current account (panel 9)? [Try it →](#c=CHN&y=1997-2031&p=si){.snap-try}
9. **Surplus and deficit.** Germany has run a current account surplus since the early 2000s and the United States a deficit. Which one lends to the rest of the world? [Try it →](#c=DEU,USA,CHN&y=1995-2031&p=ca){.snap-try}
:::

## Notes {#notes}

**Reading the charts.**

- **Actual data and projections.** Solid lines are actual data; dotted lines are the IMF's projections.
  The IMF gives the last year of actual data for each country and indicator (often the year before the
  WEO's release; earlier for some countries), and every later year is a projection. The lighter gray
  band marks the projected years of the first country's real GDP growth. Switch **Show the IMF
  projections** off to keep only the actual data.
- **Recessions.** The darker gray bands are recessions of the first country shown: the years in which its
  real GDP fell (negative growth in panel 1).
- **Titles.** Each title gives the latest *actual* value of each series in the years shown, with its year.
  When several countries are compared, the latest values are in the legend.
- With one country, a chart with two series draws them in blue and green; panel 12 draws the second on
  its own axis on the right (a ratio scale). When several countries or groups are compared, each chart
  shows one series (choose it above the chart), with one line per country.
- **Benchmark.** The benchmark is drawn as a gray line in every chart, so a country can be read against
  it: the United States by default, or any country or group. It disappears when it is one of the
  countries shown; choose **None** to remove it.
- **Country groups.** The WEO's own aggregates (the World, advanced economies, the euro area, regions)
  can be shown and compared like countries. The IMF computes them as weighted averages of their members
  (see the WEO's statistical appendix). Some indicators exist only for some groups.
- **Average growth.** The dashed line in panel 1 is the mean of the yearly growth rates in the years
  shown (projections included when they are shown).
- Missing years are gaps in the lines. The output gap and the structural balance exist mainly for
  advanced economies; many countries have no unemployment rate.

**The variables.** The data file that the Python code reads (and that **Download CSV** gives) has one row
per country (or group), year and variable, with these columns:

| Column | Definition |
|---|---|
| `iso3` | three-letter country code (IMF), or a WEO group code (G001 = World) |
| `country` | country or group name (short form) |
| `year` | year |
| `variable` | the variable (see the table below) |
| `value` | its value |
| `status` | "actual" or "IMF projection" (the years after last_actual) |
| `last_actual` | the last year of actual data of this country and variable |
| `source` | empty for the IMF WEO; where the WEO has no number, the series that fills the gap (see below) |

and these variables, from the WEO indicators:

| Panel | Variable | Definition (WEO indicator) | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `growth` | Real GDP growth (`NGDP_RPCH`) | % per year |
| 2 | `infl` | Inflation (average) (`PCPIPCH`) | % per year (consumer prices) |
| 2 | `infl_eop` | Inflation (end of year) (`PCPIEPCH`) | % per year (consumer prices) |
| 3 | `unemp` | Unemployment rate (`LUR`) | % of the labor force |
| 4 | `gap` | Output gap (`NGAP_NPGDP`) | % of potential GDP |
| 5 | `balance` | Overall balance (`GGXCNL_NGDP`) | % of GDP |
| 5 | `primary` | Primary balance (`GGXONLB_NGDP`) | % of GDP |
| 6 | `struct` | Structural balance (`GGSB_NPGDP`) | % of potential GDP |
| 7 | `revenue` | Revenue (`GGR_NGDP`) | % of GDP |
| 7 | `spending` | Spending (`GGX_NGDP`) | % of GDP |
| 8 | `debt` | Gross debt (`GGXWDG_NGDP`) | % of GDP |
| 8 | `net_debt` | Net debt (`GGXWDN_NGDP`) | % of GDP |
| 9 | `ca` | Current account (`BCA_NGDPD`) | % of GDP |
| 10 | `saving` | National saving (`NGSD_NGDP`) | % of GDP |
| 10 | `investment` | Investment (`NID_NGDP`) | % of GDP |
| 11 | `exports` | Exports (`TX_RPCH`) | % change in volume |
| 11 | `imports` | Imports (`TM_RPCH`) | % change in volume |
| 12 | `ppp_share` | Share of world GDP (`PPPSH`) | % of world GDP (PPP) |
| 12 | `ppp_pc` | GDP per capita (`PPPPC`) | international dollars (PPP, current prices) |
| | `pop` | Population (`LP`), in the page's heading | millions |

**Rebuild a chart in Python.** Open **Show the Python code** under any chart. The code reflects what the
page shows (the countries, the benchmark, the years and the projections), uses only pandas and Plotly
Express, and reads the data file from the book's GitHub repository, so it runs in any empty Colab
notebook. Change the choices in Step 2 and run the cell again. The data file is
[weo_snapshots.csv](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/main/data/snapshots/weo_snapshots.csv), described in its [README](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/snapshots/WEO_README.md).

**Updates.** The IMF publishes a new *World Economic Outlook* every April and October, and revises both
its projections and the past data. These snapshots use the October 2026 release.
